WINCHESTER, TENN., June 18.—Between midnight and day this morning Mattie Vaughan, a white woman of this place, was aroused by a voice saying that they had a note for her. She states that she arose and opened the door, when Henry Huddleston, a colored vagabond, seized her and outraged her person twice. The alarm was given this morning, when a crowd started in pursuit. He was found about five miles north of here in the house of a negro. Huddleston was seen yesterday on the street drunk, and left Arledge's saloon last night at about 11 in a drunken condition. He was placed under guard in the courthouse yard. Considerable excitement prevailed.

At about 9:30 p.m. a crowd of men suddenly broke in on the guards, blew out the light, seized the prisoner, carried him from the room in the courthouse, where he was confined, and took him to a tree in the courthouse yard, where he was lynched. Everything was done in a quick, yet determined manner. In a conversation with Huddleston about dark, he said he knew he would be hung, but denied his guilt. The tree on which he was hung is the same that Dotson was hung on in 1866.

Monday morning past the lifeless body of Henry Huddleston, a negro, was found suspended to a limb of one of the trees in the Courtyard of Winchester. A piece of paper was attached to his body, upon which was written the following:

"When a man tires of life let him follow the example of deceased, and sure death. LYNCH."

A jury of inquest was held, and the following opinion was rendered:

State of Tennessee, Franklin county.—An inquisition holden at Winchester, in the county of Franklin and State aforesaid, on the 19th day of June, 1882, before N. R. Martin, a Justice of the Peace of said county, upon the body of Henry Huddleston, col., there lying dead, by the jurors whose names are hereunto subscribed, who, upon their oaths, do say that the said Henry Huddleston, col., came to his death by hanging by the hands of unknown parties.

In testimony whereof the said jurors have hereunto set their hands the day and date above.

R. G. Smith, P. H. Plemons,
G. R. Martin, J. C. Hopkins,
C. F. Gattis, John Burrough,
J. A. Kight, Clarence Horne.

Henry Huddleston was in his 22d year, able-bodied, worthless and of bad character. He was often drunk and often in fusses and fights. Last Saturday night, about half-past ten o'clock, he went to the house of Mrs. Matt Vaughan in Winchester, and by a plausible fabrication as to his intentions succeeded in gaining admission. When Mrs. V. suspected his designs she ordered him to get out of her house, whereupon he seized her and dragged her out doors. With his hand upon her throat he outraged her and then took her into the house and repeated the outrage as often as he pleased. A heavy storm of wind and rain was raging, which drowned the cries of Mrs. Vaughan and her little child for help. Besides, the fiend threatened to kill her and her child if they made any more noise, or they ever told upon him. It was one or two o'clock Sunday morning when he left. As soon as daylight came Mrs. Vaughan sent for different parties, to whom she related all the circumstances. Of course much excitement followed, and soon our officers and a number of other persons were searching in every direction for the racal He was found about five miles from town, by Mr. James C. Arledge, and brought to town. He was carried in the presence of Mrs. Vaughan, who was on her bed at home. She there identified the negro and repeated the whole matter again exactly as before. She knew him well. He only lived about five hundred yards from her house. Without giving details, we will say that the guilt of the negro was apparent to all. In fact, we never knew so much overwhelming proof of guilt. He was kept guarded in the Courtyard until night, when he was taken to a room in the Courthouse. At about 9 o'clock p.m. a crowd of men bursted open the doors, rushed upon the guards, blew out the light, seized the prisoner and took him to a tree and hung him.

THE ODESSA OUTRAGE
NO NEW DEVELOPMENTS IN THE CASE—A PRELIMINARY HEARING BEFORE MAGISTRATE VAN DYKE.

There seem to be no new developments in the dastardly outrage that was committed near Odessa, on Thursday afternoon last, beyond those fully given in the GAZETTE of Saturday.

The licherous fiend was given a hearing at 9 o'clock on Friday evening before Esquire VanDyke, of Fdessa, at which the little victim of the foul deed, related, between her uncontrollable sobs, the story of the crime, and also positively identified the inhuman wretch.

Elias Pryor, colored, testified to seeing the prisoner at the door of the victim's father, as he was passing, the prisoner called to him saying: "Hello, old man." He could not be mistaken in the man.

Charles Bristor, colored, testified to seeing the prisoner approaching the house where the crime was committed. This completed the evidence and the prisoner was committed without bail.

While Deputy Sheriff Pennington waiting with his prisoner at Middletown for the train threats of lynching were fircely made and at one time it looked as though the threats would be carried into execution. The only thing that unfortunately prevented it was the moving off of the train.

When the facts of the crime became known a vigilance committee was at once formed and started in search of the foul fiend. After a search of many hours they succeeded in capturing him yesterday afternoon.

THE VICTIM.

The victim of the foul deed is a little thirteen year old daughter of Henry Perce, who resides in a tenant house on the farm of the venerable Bishop Scott, near Odessa. The fiend is a burly negro known by the name of James Loat, who was employed on one of the adjoining farms.
THE CRIME COMMITTED.

On Thursday morning last the father and mother of the victim, who are poor people, and obliged to eke out an existence by day's work, after bidding their daughter good bye and admonishing her to be careful, left what was at that time thier happy home for their respective places of labor. They departed in full confidence of the safety of their children, and little did they think at the time that a slimy snake would crawl into their happy home and sting their o dest daughter with its foul poison.

About 4 o'clock in the afternoon, the black fiend called at the home, and upon knocking, was answered by the daughter left in charge. He inquired for her father and being that he was not at home, put the same question in regard to her mother and received the same answer.

Being apparently satisfied that no one was at home to protect the defenceless girl, he boldly stepped into the house, despite all efforts of the daughter to prevent him. She at once attempted to give an alarm but was prevented from doing so by the fiend clapping one of his hands over her mouth. After having stopped the child's cries he, despite her struggles, threw her upon the floor and committed the fiendish crime.

THE ESCAPE.

After having accomplished the crime the negro fled, leaving his victim lying upon the flyor helpless. No one was present to help her in her helplessness. When her father returned from his day's labor she was sufficiently recovered to relate the circumstances, and give a description of the foul villain.

A VIGILANCE COMMITTEE.

The father almost dumbfounded and staggering under the great blow, started at once for Odessa, about 1½ miles away, to give the alarm. Arriving there he at once told his tale of woe to a party of men. A vigilant party was at once formed and after procuring a double team, attached to a large wagon, they started in pursuit and continued it until yesterday afternoon, when the villain was captured. The party with their prisoner at once drove to Odessa, and there being no other convenient place, the negro was confined in the cellar of Paullin's hotel, and guarded by a number of the men.

THREATS OF LYNCHING

Threats of lynching the black fiend were freely made, and it even went so far that a party was forming to do it, but some of the members backed out. Probably it might have been done had it not been for the arrival of Ash Pennington, Deputy Sheriff, who took charge of the prisoner. This morning Mr. Pennington brought his prisoner to New Castle on the train leaving Middletown at 11.07.

The victim is suffering greatly and is not expected to live.

Mr. Prettyman was an industrious and earnest worker, and was somewhat noted as a revivalist. He was well-known in Pennsylvania and throughout the Peninsula. ANOTHER OUTRAGE.—A Negro of Appoquinimink Commits an Unnamed Outrage upon a Little Girl.—Another of those detestable outrages called rape and which of late have become so painfully common in the lower part of New Castle co., was perpetrated by a negro on a little white girl in Appoquinimink Hundred about a mile and a half from Odaessa, on Thursday afternoon.

The name of the fiend who committed the outrage is James Redden, about 25 years of age and who resides with his father in a tenement house on the farm of Bishop Scott. The name of the victim of the negro's brutal passions is Sallie Purse, aged about 14 years daughter of William H. Purse, a respectable and respected citizen residing between Bishop Scott's farm and Odessa.

When the negro accomplished his fiendish purpose the family were absent from home except the girl and an infant. Information was given to the parents on their return home and the news being communicated to the neighbors a search was commenced for the negro who from the description given by the girl was believed to be Redden. The victim was terribly abused, but is much better. The search for the negro was kept up unremittingly and Friday evening he was arrested in J. D. Armstrong's store at Middletown.

Loud talk of lynching the villain was common in Middletown, and Constable Pennington who had the wretch in charge, had to use great precaution to keep his prisoner from being violently dealt with. On being taken before Esquire Vandyke, the little girl, who had been sent for, recognized him as the negro who had committed the outrage. Saturday morning Redden, in charge of Constable Pennington, was taken up to New Castle and lodged in jail to await trial at the May term of Court.

Redden though young, is an acknowledged outlaw. He is charged with having some two years ago decoyed a tramp into the woods near Middletown, where he assaulted, robbed him and left him for dead. He got clear through insufficient proof of the crime.

In an altercation with his father that morning, whose head he cut with a knife, he was shot in the wrist where the ball still remains. He claims he can prove an alibi.

A few months ago, when William Neal, upon whom was proven a clear case of rape, was turned out unpunished upon society, it was predicted that similar outrages upon defenseless white women would speedily follow, and the predictions were well founded. The outrage is one of the most nefarious of its kind ever committed in this State, and that its perpetrator was not promptly strung up on a limb of some handy tree to kick at indefinite space, speaks strongly for the forbearance of Odessa people, and proves that they have not lost all faith in the courts of their State. The evidence against Redden seems overwhelmingly conclusive, and he will doubtless be promptly tried, convicted and executed. Should his neck be saved by such means as were resorted to in the case of the negro Neal, no remedy will be left the people for the protection of their wives and daughters but a resort to the Court of Judge Lynch.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A9:
The Odessa Outrage.
little more than a mile from the
A little more than a mile from the town of Odessa, on the road leading to Fieldsboro, and at the gate of Mr. George L. Townsend, there lives in a small one story tenement house, Henry Purse, his wife and two children. The family is poor, and Purse is much away from home at labor. The eldest child, Sarah, is a bright, intelligent girl, about 14 years old, though, being of slight stature, she does not appear to an observer to be more than thirteen. The younger child is about three years old. On Thursday afternoon of last week, whilst Purse was away at work in the neighborhood of Snyrna, and Mrs. Purse at the house of a neighbor, the two children being alone, James Redden (alias Loat), a worthless negro of notorious character, entered the house and committed a felonious outrage upon the oldest girl. The details of such crimes cannot be printed in a decent newspaper, and decent people have no desire to read them. The child was left bruised, stunned, and frightened almost out of her wits. The condition in which her mother found her upon returning home attested to the fearful manner in which she had been mal-treated by the black-hearted as well as black-skinned and beastly scoundrel. Her husband being absent, Mrs. Purse hardly knew what to do, upon first learning of the outrage, but finally decided to go to Fieldsboro and ask the advice of Henry Willard. He advised her to say nothing further of the outrage until her husband returned. Mr. Purse came home late Friday evening, but in the meantime rumors of the outrage had reached Odessa and a search was being made for the villain. The girl did not know her assailant, and a clue to his identity was obtained through Charles Bristor, a negro, who, while coming from Fieldsboro, saw Redden at a window of Purse's house. This occurred, it is believed, before the assault was committed. Obtaining this important information from Bristor, Alexander Moody and Alfred Stevens went in search of Redden, found him in front of J. G. Armstrong's store, and secured him. He was then taken to Purse's in a carriage but was not taken in the presence of Sarah until she had given a detailed description of her assailant. Redden corresponded exactly to her description, even to that of a large ring upon one of his fingers. Being taken before her she instantly recognised him as the man who had assaulted her. He was then taken back to Odessa and confined in a room in Paullin's Hotel. There was no movement to lynch him, as reported by Wilmington reporters who sat in Wilmington and wrote up the details of the affair, "hit or miss." The quiet and order-loving people of Odessa seemed to have faith that the villian would get a just amount of hanging by due process of law. Deputy Sheriff Ash Pennington went to Odessa early Saturday morning and took charge of Redden. He was taken before Esquire Vandyke, who after hearing the testimony of the victim of the outrage, and Dr. Woods, and two colored men—Bristor and Frisby Lloyd—who saw the prisoner at the house of Purse, held him for court. Ash Pennington brought him to Middletown after the hearing and took him to New Castle on the 11 o'clock train. He is now behind the bars, and, it is said, has gone to praying loudly for his soul. The reports in the Wilmington papers that an attempt was made at Middletown to lynch the villian are utterly without foundation. If Middletown people had undertaken the job they would have carried it through. Redden is a negro of notorious reputation. A few years ago he nearly killed a white boy without the least provocation, but by some means escaped punishment.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A10:
An Atrocious Crime.
One of the atrocious crimes known to the calendar, is charged to have been committed by a colored man, known as James Redden, near Odessa, Delaware, on Thursday of last week. The facts as given are as follows: Upon the day named, Redden, who also owns the alias of "Loot," visited the house of Henry Purse, on the suburbs of the village of Odessa, during the absence of all the adult members of the family.

Purse's fourteen year old daughter was at home tending the younger children when the negro arrived. After ascertaining that the girl's parents were absent, the villain caught her by the arms and, stifling her mouth, committed a beastly assault. The child's father returned, and ascertained from the neighbors that the man had been in the neighborhood, but none had guessed the repulsive nature of his errand. The girl, when questioned, related the circumstances to her father, and the news of the crime spread through the town rapidly, and the citizens were frenzied with indignation and excitement. A warrant was sworn out for Redden's arrest, and he was taken into custody while entering a store in Odessa.

THE OUTRAGED CITIZENS GATHER.

He was confined in a private house over night, and an organized band of men visited the place for the purpose of lynching the negro, but his place of concealment could not be ascertained. The next morning he was removed from the house to the depot, and but for the timely arrival of the train which carried him to New Castle jail, he would have been mobbed—the band of lynchers ran madly to the train, too late to secure the prisoner. Redden is now confined the New Castle jail, and stoutly denies the charge upon which he is held. The negro is positively identified by the outraged girl and two neighbors who saw him in the vicinity of the house. The girl suffers severely, and it is feared is seriously injured by the rufian, and the event has caused the greatest excitement in the neighborhood.

Redden is the same individual who was some time ago arrested on the charge of assaulting and badly beating a pedlar, and shortly afterward attempting to kill his own father, escaping with little or no punishment in both cases.

jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A12:
Democratic Hypocrisy.
From Middletown Transcript.

Two of the Wilmington evening papers rather overdid themselves in the way of sensation in reporting the Odessa outrage. Readers would have a better opinion of newspapers if they would get the facts in such cases and stick to them. There was no attempt made here to lynch Redden, and probably not a dozen persons in Middletown knew that he was to be taken to New Castle on the noon train of Saturday. There was no unusual crowd at the station, and there was not the least disposition shown to open court with Judge Lynch on the bench. Had the circumstances of his atrocious crime and the fact that he was to be taken to New Castle on the train been generally known here, the state of affairs at the station might have been more exciting. But perhaps it is best as it is.

The two evening papers alluded to in the above article were the Democratic Every evening and Gazette, and the articles were no doubt penned by their young and enterprising reporters.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A17:
THE GALLOWS.
JAMES REDDEN PAYS THE
DEATH PENALTY OF
VIOLATED LAW.
THE CRIME.
THE CRIME.

The crime for which James Redden suffered the extreme penalty of the law was committed on the morning of the 23d of last February. His victim, little Sallie Purse, who was then about 13 years of age, being alone in the house, with the exception a baby sister, about 2 years of age. The house where the outrage was committed, is situated on the road between Odessa and Fielssboro. The father had been away for a couple of days, and the mother had gone that morning, immediately after breakfast, to see a sick person, leaving Sallie to wash the dishes and straighten up the house. About 9 o'clock Redden came along and after entering the house asked the girl to give him something to eat. Not having anything cooked she baked him some cakes, fried some meat and made some coffee. When he was done eating he went to the door and after looking up and down the road returned, and seizing hold of the child threw her on the floor, at the same time telling her "if you holler, I'll kill you," accompanying the threat with a motion as though he was about to draw a knife from his pocket.

THE ARREST.

After the foul death had been consummated he remained in the house for several hours, and then threatening her with death in case she told her mother, he took his departure. While he was in the house two colored men passed along the road and he spoke to one of them. When Mrs. Purse returned in the evening, Sallie told her what had happened but it was some time before the mother could believe it. The next day Mr. Purse returned, but before he reached home heard of the affair which by that time was pretty well known all over the country. The father had a warrant issued immediately, and Redden was arrested the same evening while holding a horse in front of Vandyke's store. He was taken to the house of Mr. Purse, and fully identified by Sallie as her assailant. The next day he was taken to New Castle where he was kept until the May term of Court when he was brought to this city for trial.

THE TRIAL AND CONVICTION.

When the case was called Harry Sharpley, Esq., was appointed by the Court to defend him. After a delay of several days, during which Mr. Sharpley was using every means in his power to obtain witnesses who would be able to clear his client of the horrid crime with which he was charged the trial was commenced.

The prisoner plead not guilty, and after some fifteen challenges had been made a jury consisting of 11 white men and 1 colored man was secured. The evidence was direct and convincing, that of his victim, who broke down several times on the stand, especially so. The defence endeavored to prove an alibi, but utterly tailed in the attempt and the few witnesses that were examined only tended to show still further that he was at the house the time the offense was committed. The counsel on both sides made able arguments, and the jury after being charged by the Chief Justice, retired at noon on the second day of the trial. The evidence was so clear that it was not expected they would be out more than a few hours, but contrary to all expectation it was 19 hours before they arrived at a verdict. They came into Court on the morning of the second day for instructions, and about an hour afterwards returned with a verdict of guilty. Immediately after the verdict was rendered Court adjourned until 3 o'clock in the afternoon. During the recess the prisoner was removed to one of the cells in the basement of the Court House, and made no hesitation in confessing his guilt and saying that all the girl had said was true.
At 3 o'clock in the afternoon of the same day he was again brought into Court and the Chief Justice after dwelling on the enormity of the crime, and picturing the blasted life of this innocent child, sentenced him to be hung on the 25th of August.

HOW HE PASSED THE TIME.

After his sentence he was removed to New Castle jail in a close carriage. He has been quiet and orderly, and ate his meals with a relish that seemed strangely in keeping with the position in which he was placed. He was frequently visited by Rev. Dr. Spotswood, a colored preacher and other friends. He learned to read and seemed to take great pleasure in reading the Bible. His mother is a constant visitor and has always tried to give him encouragement and consolation. Although she always seemed calm an observer could not fail to see that it was only by a great effort she concealed her emotions while she was in his presence. On several occasions he has confessed that he did wrong and was sorry for it.

THE EXECUTION.

Redden was executed at 10.21 this morning. The Sheriff cut the rope and his feet touched the ground. At 10.26 the movement of the heart ceased.

THE NEGRO REDDEN, WHO COMMITTED A RAPE ON A LITTLE GIRL, HANGED TO-DAY.
NEW CASTLE, DELI August 25 James Redden
THE NEGRO REDDEN, WHO COMMITTED A RAPE ON A LITTLE GIRL, HANGED TO-DAY.

NEW CASTLE, DEL., August 25.—James Redden, the negro hanged here to-day for rape on a 12-year old white girl, named Sallie Purse, near Odessa, last February, passed a very restless night, praying and walking the floor, until 3 o'clock this morning, when he fell asleep and rested for an hour and a half. For breakfast he ate beef, fried eggs, bread and milk, and ice cream. He wept at times during yesterday and last night. Yesterday afternoon he was visited by two clergymen, who spent half an hour with him. His mother, who was to have visited him yesterday, failed to arrive. From 9 o'clock this morning up to the hour of his execution Redden was closeted in his cell with the Revs. Nicholas M. Brown, of New Castle, and Wesley J. Parker (colored), pastor of Ezion M. E. church, Wilmington. They prayed with him, and he joined, in a steady voice, in singing "Salvation's Free" and several other hymns. At 10:12 the prisoner, preceded by the Rev. Mr. Brown, and followed by the Rev. Mr. Parker, Warden Hance, Sheriff Clark and his son, George Clark, ascended the scaffold with a firm step and took his place on the trap. Rev. Parker offered up a short prayer, after which the noose was adjusted, the black cap drawn over the prisoner's face, his ankles pinioned and, without saying a word to those assembled, he was launched into eternity at 10:17. He died easily of strangulation in 11 minutes. The execution was witnessed only by the officers of the jail, two physicians, two clergymen, the jurors and press representatives, and one woman who manifested a strong disposition to see a man hung.

The following is a history of the case: James Redden, who was also known previous to his arrest as "Jim Loat," was a full-blooded negro, about 21 years old, and slightly under the medium stature. His face was beardless and somewhat stupid and sullen in its habitual expression. He had lived around Odessa, in the central part of this county, most all his life, and had earned a reputation for general good-for-nothingness and an ugly disposition. Besides some petty offenses, he was charged with having, some two years ago, decoyed a drunken tramp into the woods, robbed him and beaten him in a dangerous manner. On Thursday, February 231, of the present year, Redden entered the house of Henry Purse, a tenant of the late Bishop Scott, one-and-a-half miles below Odessa, during the absence of Purse and his wife, who had gone out to their daily labor learning the
entered the house of Henry Purse, a tenant of the late Bishop Scott, one-and-a-half miles below Odessa, during the absence of Purse and his wife, who had gone out to their daily labor, leaving the house in charge of their daughter Sallie, a girl of between 12 and 13 years. Sallie and her baby sister were the only inmates. The negro asked the little girl for something to eat, which she prepared and set before him. Having eaten, he lingered in the house for three hours, and during that time forcibly outraged Sallie, who resisted with all her feeble strength. Redden was arrested in Odessa the evening of the following day, with some difficulty gotten out of town, and lodged in New Castle jail on Saturday morning. Threats of lynching were made, public reeling being intensified by the memory of the Neal case, but the crowd lacked a leader.

On the 24th of May, the case was called for trial in the court sitting in this city, and, after some delay, a jury was empanneled, made up of eleven white and one colored men, the latter being the first negro juror who ever sat in a capital case in this state. Harry Sharpley, esq., was assigned by the court as counsel for the prisoner, and he entered into the defense so earnestly as to draw from some of his party (the democratic) unfavorable criticism for excess of zeal. But the evidence was too strong to be shaken, and the jury, after deliberating twenty-four hours, and balloting sixteen times for a verdict, found the prisoner guilty in manner and form as indicted. Redden listened to his trial and the sentence which followed close thereafter with stolic indifference, and did not seem to the observers to realize that his life had been forfeited. While awaiting his execution he maintained the same dogged indifference to his approaching doom, rarely referring to it, and still more rarely exhibiting any emotion. He was visited several times by his mother and sister, and frequently by members of the New Castle clergy, both white and colored, in whose conversation and prayers he seemed to take much comfort. He talked freely about his crime, but always stoutly maintained that it was nothing more than seduction, and that he committed no assault.

CHICAGO, June 1. — A terrible riot occurred this evening at Brighton Park, five miles south of this city, where the iron works of the Joliet Iron and Steel company are located. The company has been employing men from Joliet. This evening while 15 workmen were on the train proceeding home, about 100 strikers rushed aboard the train armed with pistols, knives, clubs and strips of iron, and commenced a murderous attack upon all passengers. Judge Pittsburg, of Pontiac, was shot through the hip and dangerously wounded. Four colored non-union men were terribly and fatally beaten, and many passengers badly wovnded.

Judge Pittsburg is judge of the second district appellate court, and was a passenger on the Chicago & Alton train proceeding home at Pontiac. He is universally respected, and the rioters certainly could have no spite against him, but the hundred infuriated workers belonging to the union rushed madly through the cars, shooting right and left, and clubbing everybody or slashing them with knives. All the passengers were more or less wounded, but none fatally, except Judge Pittsburg and the four colored non-union iron workers. Judge Pittsburg was brought to this city, and physicians probed unsuccessfully for the ball which lodged in the ilum. Subsequently the judge was conveyed on the midnight train to his home in a very critical condition.

The four colored men who were so terribly beaten were also taken to their homes at Joliet on the same train, and will probably die. It seems the object of the rioters was to intimidate the scabs who had taken the places of strikers at the mills. When the evening train first stopped at Brighton Park station, several rioters boarded the cars, and with pistols intimidated the engineer to hold the train until the murderous work was accomplished. Rioters boarded the cars, and with pistols intimidated the engineer to hold the train until the murderous work was accomplished. A large force of police repaired to the scene later, and at midnight had arrested several of the rioters.

Eye-witnesses state the attack of the rioters was so sudden and savage that the wildest confusion prevailed among the passengers. The hundred rioters dashed into the smoking-car and coaches, yelling like demons, and brandishing pistols, bowie-knives, crow bars, clubs and all sorts of weapons. joliet-strikers-chicago-1882-06-01.A8:
A DASTARDLY OUTBAGE.
Yesterday's Chicago papers are filled with columns of details of one of the most dastardly outrages ever perpetrated outside of Jessie James's kingdom. "From the character of the affair," says the Chicago Times, "it would seem that a section of Missouri had been brought up into Illinois and planted in Cook county. For border rufflanism it could not be equalled by New Mexican cowboys."

The facts in brief are as follows: For the past two weeks the Joliet Iron and Steel company has been taking men up from Joliet to Chicago to unload iron from the vessels at its docks in that city, and taking them home each evening. The strikers have tried to break up this sort of thing, and failed, but on Thursday evening a mob of about fifty congregated at the crossing of the Alton and Pan Handle railroads in Brighton, an outlying portion of the city, and, boarding the outgoing accommodation train, which was taking about twenty of the "scabs" home, dragged eight or ten of them from the cars and beat them shamefully, fracturing a Swede's skull and clubbing and stamping a half a dozen negroes. During the melee, which occurred inside the city limits at 5:30 in the afternoon, many shots were fired by the desperadoes. One of the bullets struck Judge N. J. Pillsbury, of Pontiac, one of the appellate judges of the Ottawa circuit, inflicting a dangerous and possibly fatal wound in the left groin. The judge was a passenger on the train, and did not leave his seat. The Judge was taken from the train to the Washington hotel where he was attended by a couple of surgeons, who found that the ball had entered at the top of the left hip, at what they called the superior spinal process of the ilium, had glanced from that bone and passed down just over the hip joint and in bedded itself in the gluteal muscles of the back. The wounded man was put under the influence of ether, and the surgeons probed for the ball but failed to find it. They did not, however, consider the wound as very dangerous, and he was able to proceed to his home by the 11 o'clock train the same night.

After the outrage was over the assailants walked away in a body leisurely, for a little distance, and then scattered like sheep, firing their revolvers as they went. They disappeared as they came, no one knowing exactly how, the engineer meantime pulling up his train to the station to enable the surgeons to remove Judge Pullsbury and the rest of the wounded. Subsequently the police made four or five arrests, but there is no certainty that any of them are the right men.

THE JOLIET OUTRAGE.
Arrest of Several of the Train Rioters.
CHICAGO, June 2.—The attack of dock laborers at Bridgeport last night, upon the Chicago and Alton train, was well executed and evinced careful planning. They were thoroughly armed with sticks, clubs, pieces of iron and stone, and the number of broken and bruised heads attest their effectiveness. Three had their skulls laid bare by vicious blows and half a dozen others are crippled or hurt in various degrees. None of the injured are likely to die, even Judge Pillsbury, who was shot, being in a fair way to recover at last accounts. The riots quickly died when their vengeance was satisfied. The police were early on the scene, and have made several arrests, including James O'Brien, John O'Neill and John Frawley, all on suspicion.

A dispatch from Dwight says one of the rioters was hit accidentally in the forehead.
Daniel McWilliams, who was with Judge Pillsbury, says the shot which struck him was fired from inside the car, but none of his party saw the man who fired it. It is believed, however, that important clues are in the hands of the police, and the miscreants will be brought to justice.

SOME OF THE RIOTERS IDENTIFIED. joliet-strikers-chicago-1882-06-01.A13:
Works Attacked on a Chicago & Alton Train at Brighton Park—Three Negroes Taken from the Cars and Brutally Beaten—Judge Pillsbury Shot and Seriously Wounded.

Striking dock hands lately in the employ of the Joliet Iron & Steel Company boarded a train of the Chicago, Alton & St. Louis Railroad at Brighton Station, about five miles from this city, last evening shortly before six o'clock, and attacked a gang of "scab" laborers, white and colored, who were on their way to Joliet from Bridgeport wharf. Judge Pillsbury, of the 2d District Appellate Court, was shot seriously, if not fatally, in the groin, and three negroes and one white laborer were so terribly beaten with iron bars and stones that the recovery of at least two of them is doubtful.

The attack was planned and executed with consummate skill both as to place and time. The spot chosen is where the Alton road crosses the Pan-Handle line. All trains are compelled to halt there until the "all-right" signal has been given by the flagman. Off to the right is a Y, on which stock-yard trains change ends. From Western avenue to the railway station, perhaps 200 yards distant, the road lies through an avenue of trees thick enough to obstruct a view of the track from the adjacent houses. Moreover the road makes a short curve there. The Y is laid on a bank four feet above the bottom of the ditch, and it is believed that the conspirators hid themselves in it awaiting the approach of their victims. At all events, the telegraph operator, switchman and flagman at the crossing say they noticed no unusual number of men around until not more than five minutes before the Dwight accommodation train, which leaves the depot at Van Buren and Clark streets, was due.

As the train came in sight around the curve, the road-bed in a moment swarmed with rough-looking fellows, who, as the train halted, jumped upon the engine and presented pistols at the heads of Jones, the engineer, and the fireman and ordered them to bring the train to a dead halt. Others took position at the rear of the tender, and provided against the possibility of the train running away from them by drawing out the coupling-pin. The obnoxious seabs were known to be in the rear car, which has been attached at Bridgeport since the strikers have been resorting to violence. Into this car, by way of both doors, selected parties of the mob poured, armed with iron bars, stones and pistols. The workmen were attacked and beaten without mercy. Some who endeavored to escape through the windows and doors were assailed by the strikers, who held the track on both sides of the cars. Stones and clubs were rained upon them as they ran the gauntlet around the cars, in vain efforts to break through the lines. How any of them passed through the ordeal is the most wonderful part of it. Judge Pillsbury, who had gone into the car with a party of friends, and was playing eucher when the mob entered, arose to see what the riot was about, and had just got clear of his seat when he heard the sound of the pistol and felt the bullet. His injury was so bewildering to him and to his friends that they lost account of what was going on inside the car, remembering only the fierce yells of the infuriated assailants, and the terrified or agonized shrieks of the assailed and injured men. How long the assault lasted no one could reasonably correctly estimate. PITTSBURGH, June 21.—There is probably no man in the city to-day who could say more on an interesting topic than President Jarrett, of the Amalgamated Association. He has just returned from an extended and eventful trip throughout the West, has started up the Cincinnati iron works, has conferred with labor and capital in that city and St. Louis and Joliet, Ills., and Chicago and Cleveland, and places of lesser note, and reached home last evening, tired, but apparently in good humor with himself and the rest of Amalgamated mankind.

To-day Mr. Jarrett was found in the inner office of the Association, an interested spectator in the doings of the Committee on Revision. That body, with Secretary Martin, had reduced itself to shirt sleeves and absorption in the work before them. It was no place for reporters. And yet there was Mr. Jarrett with a brain as full of interesting material as is the Warren county pebble rock of oil. It was a tantalizing sight.

"I do not think it would be right to express my views of the general situation out West, or, in fact, to say anything for the press. In fact, silence is extremely golden in this case."

"The manufacturers here, Mr. Jarrett, are inclined to feel aggrieved, to say the least of it, that idle mills should start up in the wake of your recent trip."

"They should not feel so; a contract is a contract and must be observed. The men had bound themselves, at Cincinnati, by an agreement, and were advised to hold themselves thereto. The honor of this Association had to be maintained. That is all there is about it."

"How about the riots at Chicago and Cleveland?"

"The trouble near Chicago was in no way chargeable to any of the members of this Association. That unfortunate affair in which Judge Pillsbury was wounded, grew out of the lawless conduct of some colored non-union iron workers from Joliet, Ill."

At this juncture, Secretary Martin said briskly, "Let's get to work, boys," and as the writer was, unfortunately, not one of the boys, the hint was taken, and the Committee and the President and the Secretary were left to their labors in the cosy back parlor.

Murder of Miss Serena Benton.

Miss Serena J. Benton, a most worthy and respectable maiden lady, some sixty years of age, was brutally and foully murdered last Thursday morning in the broad light of day, some twenty-five steps from the public road, between the McNeil place and the Walton place, five miles west of Booneville. Miss Benton has been living in this part of the State for over forty years. She formerly taught school, supported herself and with the proceeds of her labor, bought her a farm upon which she was living, with her tenants, at the time of her death. Tuesday night of last week she staid at Mr. Bud Keistler's; Wednesday night, at Blake Davis's, all her neighbors. Thursday morning, after an early breakfast, she started to see Mr. George Michael, who had agreed to lend her some money. Mr. Michael not being at home, she left with the intention of going next to Mr. Bud Keistler's to get a book. She never reached Mr. Keistler's. On her way she passed the Walton place and was seen by Mrs. Daniel Michael as she passed. When last seen she was in the road about a hundred yards from the scene of the murder. Her not appearing at home created no uneasiness, as she was in the habit of staying several days at a time with her neighbors, so no search was made for the body. Last Monday the body was discovered by a negro, L. Simmons, who was attracted to the spot by a large number of buzzards. The neighbors soon assembled, sent for the coroner and guarded the remains all night, which were in a very thick cluster of bushes some twenty-five steps from the road. Tuesday morning we got in a buggy with Mr. George Collins and visited the place. A most horrible sight met the gaze. Language is inadequate to describe it, and we will draw the veil of silence over it. She had evidently been seized by the demons in the road and forced to the place where the murder was committed. A large stick found on the spot and broken into three pieces was one of the weapons used. The skull was examined by Dr. W. A. Taylor and found to be fractured, one fracture extending nearly from one ear to the other, with a double fracture on each side of the median line. This is one of the most revolting and horrid murders ever recorded in the annals of crime. The evidence is circumstantial. There is a mystery overhanging it which we hope will be cleared up and the perpetrators brought to justice. An inquest was held on Tuesday and the evidence not being finished adjourned over till Wednesday. Special to the Vicksburg Herald.
BOONEVILLE, June 17.—Some weeks ago a very estimable old lady, Miss Salina Benton, was foully murdered about five miles west of this place, and at the time suspicions rested on Morgan Hamilton, colored, as being one of the murderers. He was arrested and examined by the jury of inquest, and although there was a little circumstantial evidence against him, the jury did not consider it enough to call for a bond and he was discharged. Yesterday, however, it seems that some of the people thought that Hamilton was guilty and swore out an affidavit before G. C. Walters, J. P., and he issued a warrant for his arrest this morning. Eight men went to the field where Hamilton was at work to execute the warrant, and without any excuse, as your correspondent learns, told him to run, and as he started off, shot him dead. The Sheriff is out there now intent upon arresting the parties. The good citizens of the county are not in sympathy with this outrage, and the general hope is that all concerned in the killing may have justice meted out to them.

Saturday morning a body of ten men having a warrant issued by G. C. Walter J. P., for the arrest of Morgan Hamilton, colored, charged with complicity in the killing of Miss Serena Benton, who was murdered some three weeks ago five miles west of this place, proceeded to the field where the negro was at work and easily effected his arrest. Upon their way to the justice the negro ran off and at the distance of fifteen or twenty paces, his body was riddled with thirty-four bullets two of the party using shot guns and one a pistol. After being shot he ran some 150 yards pursued by one of the party on foot, fell and expired in a few minutes. One of the squads was not present at the shoot- ang. This boy had before been arre- tested and brought before the jury of inquest held over the body of Miss Benton. The witnesses against him and he himself were rigidly examined at the request of the jury by B. A. P. Selman, Esq., and his innocence being established in the estimation of the jury, he was released. What new evidence was found against him to justify his re- arrest we know not. It is even reported that he was told by 'some of the party to run, and having done so, was shot. The Sheriff proceeded to the scene of the killing on Saturday to arrest the parties but they had fled and no arrests have been made. We have given the facts of this case as near as we have been able to procure them and will let the public form their own conclusions. These violations of the law are to be regretted, and the guilty ones when ascertained, should be punished as the law directs.—Beoneville Pleader, 22d.
